chapter_theme: Not desiring another man's wife, argued mostly from consequences: constant fear, small pleasure, the king's punishment, family disgrace, hell and a degraded rebirth. The last quatrains turn from the act to desire itself, a fire worse than any outer fire, which the strong suppress in silence.
structure_note: 81 to 87 weigh the act's costs against its pleasure; 88 to 90 move to desire as an inner burning that water, hills and outer fires do not match.

81.reading: The fear is great and the pleasure small; thought through, it risks death at the king's hands and is a deed that daily sharpens toward hell, so those with a sense of shame should not set their hopes on another man's wife.
81.nuance: The case is prudential from start to finish, weighing fear against pleasure, but the appeal at the end is to shame (நாணுடையார).

82.reading: Virtue, renown, friendship and greatness do not come to those who desire another man's wife; enmity, blame, sin and fear do.

83.reading: Fear on entering, fear on returning, fear while enjoying, fear in keeping it hidden: it brings fear at every moment, so why does a man enter another's house without dread?
83.nuance: The repetition of அச்சம் enacts the condition it describes. The closing question turns on the same word: the one who lives in fear lacks the one fear that would have kept him out.

84.reading: If seen, the family is disgraced; if caught, a leg is cut off; the unmanly act itself is fear; and it yields long suffering in hell: tell me, profligate, what pleasure did you find?
84.nuance: Mudaliar reads ஆணின்மை as the absence of the qualities that make a man, so the adulterer's daring is renamed unmanliness.

85.reading: Those who in a former birth, with no sense of right and in the company of the mean, went by force to other men's wives become eunuchs in this birth and live by dancing.
85.nuance: The punishment mirrors the offence: those who used male force are reborn without it. This is the chapter's one claim about a past birth; the Kural's chapter on another's wife makes none.

86.reading: When a man has at home a tender, loving wife, married on a day fixed by asking, with drums beaten for many to know, why should he look at a stranger's wife?
86.nuance: The public wedding is the point: a bond announced to many and guarded (கடி) is set against one that has to be hidden.

87.reading: The pleasure of the unsteady-hearted man who, maddened, unites with another's wife while neighbours gossip and his own people tremble and grieve, is like licking a cobra's head.
87.nuance: The image holds pleasure and lethal danger in a single act, so no separate weighing of costs is needed.

88.reading: In the strong, the sickness of desire does not spread, show itself or settle on many; fearing shame among those outside, they say nothing and it subsides within. Oh, how cruel it is!
88.nuance: The strong are not free of desire, only able to contain it, and the cry 'how cruel' can fall on that containment. Mudaliar reads it so: desire that can't come out and must be suffered inwardly is the cruellest.

positions.position: Because it doesn't come out but stays within and subsides only after great suffering, the desire of the wise is called very cruel.

89.reading: Arrow, fire and the sun's bright rays, however they blaze, burn only the outside; desire, blazing and troubling the mind, burns the mind itself, so it is to be feared more than they.

90.reading: From a fierce red fire rising in the town one can escape by plunging into water; but desire burns even if one plunges into water, and burns even if one climbs a hill to hide.
90.nuance: Water and the hilltop are the two refuges from fire, and both fail because this fire travels with the one who flees.

links.note: 146 lists four things that never leave the adulterer: enmity, sin, fear and blame. 82 keeps the same four and pairs them with four goods he loses: virtue, renown, friendship and greatness.
148 calls not looking at another's wife great manliness (பேராண்மை); 84 calls the act unmanliness (ஆணின்மை).
Both turn on the look (நோக்கு): 148 praises the manliness that does not look at another's wife, and 86 asks why a married man would look at all.

In 1134 the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness. In 88 the strong, fearing shame, keep desire hidden until it subsides. Both make claims about whether shame can hold desire, and they answer opposite ways. The conflict depends on reading 1134 as a general claim; it is a lover's plea in the Book of Love, while 88 states a rule about the strong.
Both contrast an outer burn with an inner one: in 129 the fire's wound heals but the tongue's scar does not, and in 89 arrow, fire and sun burn the body while desire burns the mind.
Both say desire burns where fire can't: 1159 says fire burns only when touched while love burns at a distance, and 90 that fire can be escaped in water but desire can't.
The same figure in another domain: 1049 says one can sleep in the midst of fire but not of poverty, and 90 that one can escape fire but not desire. Each makes fire the lesser affliction.

source_issues: 85, 87: the Tamil has OCR errors in the அளபெடை forms (மாணஇ for மரீஇ, பாணஇ for பரீஇ, பெண்மாணஇ for பெண்மரீஇ); Mudaliar's glosses give the correct forms.
88: the Tamil's line breaks and punctuation are misplaced around ஓஓ கொடிதே. Shanmuganar's field for 88 also contains the Tamil and commentary of 89.
89: Shanmuganar's commentary is not aligned (it sits at the end of 88's field).
